# Intervention at Delegation: Can Permission Scoping at Sub-Agent Creation Time Prevent Irreversible Actions?

**Problem:** In the causal chain, the orchestrator delegates to sub-agents. If the permissions granted to sub-agents at creation time are minimally scoped, sub-agents cannot take irreversible actions even if they try.

**Direction:** Implement a delegation framework with three permission levels: (a) full tool access (baseline), (b) tools scoped to task type, (c) minimal permission set (only tools logically required for the subtask). Run 20 tasks and measure: irreversible action rate, task success rate, and false-blocking rate (times minimal permission prevents needed action).

**Why it matters:** Least-privilege delegation is a standard principle in cybersecurity. Applying it to sub-agent creation could be the most practical intervention in the causal chain with the best safety/utility tradeoff.

**Relevant context:** The causal chain specified in the prompt; principle of least privilege from computer security; NIST AI Agent Standards Initiative (nist.gov); Gravitee 2026 security report on unauthorized actions.

# Intervention Just Before Irreversible Action: Real-Time Tripwires in Agentic Pipelines

**Problem:** Even when upstream interventions fail, a last-resort check at the point of irreversible action execution could prevent harm. No standard 'tripwire' system for this exists in agent frameworks.

**Direction:** Implement a pre-execution tripwire: before each tool call, a small classifier predicts whether the action is irreversible. If classified as irreversible, the call is held for 10 seconds with a human override window. Test on 30 tasks. Measure: true positive rate (correctly held irreversible actions), false positive rate (incorrectly held reversible actions), and override usage rate.

**Why it matters:** A tripwire is the last intervention node before harm occurs. Even an imperfect tripwire with 70% recall on irreversible actions would prevent a large fraction of the most harmful agent mistakes.

**Relevant context:** The causal chain specified in the prompt; Anthropic's guidance on human approval for irreversible actions; ControlArena for testing safety protocols (apartresearch.com); METR monitorability evaluations.

# Post-Irreversible-Action Rollback: Building and Testing a Recovery Protocol When No Rollback Exists

**Problem:** The final node in the causal chain is 'no rollback possible'. While technical rollback may be impossible, a structured damage-limitation protocol may still reduce harm.

**Direction:** For 10 simulated irreversible agent actions (file deletion, sent email, executed transaction), develop and test a post-incident damage-limitation protocol (notify affected parties, document causal chain, request reversal where possible, patch vulnerability). Measure harm reduction from applying the protocol vs. no structured response.

**Why it matters:** Even when rollback is technically impossible, structured incident response can limit cascading harm. This fills the final gap in the causal chain and directly addresses the open problem of agentic incident response.

**Relevant context:** The causal chain final node in the prompt; agentic incident response as an open problem; Partnership on AI's real-time failure detection report (2025); Adversa AI incident case studies.

# Causal Chain Audit: Which Node Intervention Has the Best Safety/Utility Tradeoff?

**Problem:** Multiple intervention points exist in the agentic causal chain, but there is no empirical comparison of their relative safety benefit vs. utility cost.

**Direction:** Implement five interventions, one at each node of the causal chain (task specification, decomposition, delegation scoping, pre-execution tripwire, post-incident protocol). Run the same 20 tasks with each intervention individually and in combination. Measure safety improvement and task completion rate for each. Rank by safety/utility tradeoff.

**Why it matters:** Practitioners need to know which single intervention gives the most safety improvement per unit of utility cost. An empirical comparison would provide directly actionable guidance.

**Relevant context:** All five causal chain nodes specified in the prompt; ControlArena for testing control protocols (apartresearch.com); METR task suite for standardized task measurement.

# Measuring Whether Explicit Reversibility Awareness in the Causal Chain Prevents Compounding Failures

**Problem:** Agents that explicitly reason about reversibility at each step of the causal chain may make significantly different (and safer) delegation and action choices than agents that do not.

**Direction:** Compare two agent conditions on 25 tasks: (a) standard agent, (b) agent with explicit reversibility-awareness prompting at each decision point in the causal chain ('before delegating this subtask, consider: is this action reversible?'). Measure irreversible action rate and task quality.

**Why it matters:** If a simple prompting intervention at each causal chain node significantly reduces irreversible actions, this is immediately deployable without framework changes.

**Relevant context:** The causal chain decomposition in the prompt; Anthropic's guidance on minimal footprint and reversibility; the outcome-driven constraint violations benchmark (arxiv 2512.20798).

# Backcasting from Safe Agent Operations: What System Properties Must Be Present for All Agents to Stay Within Boundaries?

**Problem:** The success state — all AI agents operate safely within defined boundaries with no irreversible harmful actions — implies a set of necessary system properties. Identifying these properties provides a design target.

**Direction:** Conduct structured backcasting: starting from the success state, identify what properties of individual agents, communication protocols, tool systems, and oversight mechanisms are necessary conditions. Produce a formal properties checklist. Test which current agent systems satisfy what fraction of properties. Publish as a design checklist.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from success provides a positive design target rather than just a list of failures to avoid. The checklist would be immediately useful for practitioners deploying agentic systems.

**Relevant context:** The success state specified in the prompt; NIST AI Agent Standards Initiative (nist.gov, February 2026); the 2025 AI Agent Index (arxiv 2602.17753) which documents current deployment gaps.

# Minimum Viable Safety Stack: What Is the Smallest Set of Interventions That Gets Agents to 90% Boundary Compliance?

**Problem:** Full boundary compliance for AI agents likely requires many interventions. Practitioners with limited resources need to know the minimum viable set of safety measures that achieves the most safety improvement.

**Direction:** Starting from the success state, work backward to identify the interventions whose removal would cause the largest reduction in boundary compliance. Test each intervention in isolation and in combination on a standardized task suite. Produce a Pareto-optimal safety stack ranked by safety improvement per implementation hour.

**Why it matters:** For student researchers and resource-constrained practitioners, a minimum viable safety stack is more actionable than a comprehensive but unimplementable framework.

**Relevant context:** The success state in the prompt; ControlArena hackathon design (apartresearch.com); Gravitee 2026 security report showing 81% of teams lack full security approval, suggesting resource constraints.

# Gap Analysis: What Structural Changes Are Required to Move from Current to Safe Agent Operations?

**Problem:** Current agentic systems are far from the success state of full boundary compliance. A structured gap analysis would identify the most critical missing components.

**Direction:** Score 5 widely deployed agentic systems (LangChain agent, AutoGen agent, a commercial API assistant, ControlArena agent, METR evaluation agent) against the success-state properties checklist from the backcasting exercise. Quantify the gap for each system. Identify which properties are universally absent vs. sometimes present.

**Why it matters:** A gap analysis grounds safety work in the current deployment reality. Universally absent properties are the highest-priority research targets.

**Relevant context:** The 2025 AI Agent Index (arxiv 2602.17753) which systematically documents deployed agent properties; Gravitee 2026 security report; NIST AI Agent Standards Initiative.

# Designing for Reversibility: Can Safe-State Default Design Principles Be Derived from the Success State?

**Problem:** The success state implies that agents should default to safe states when uncertain. Deriving a set of concrete 'safe-state default' design principles from this success state would provide actionable design guidance.

**Direction:** Working backward from the success state, derive 10 'safe-state default' design principles (e.g., 'default to requesting human confirmation when action irreversibility is uncertain', 'default to minimal tool set'). Test each principle's effect on safety failure rate and utility on 20 tasks. Identify which principles have the best tradeoff.

**Why it matters:** Design principles derived from success-state backcasting are more likely to be coherent and mutually reinforcing than principles derived from individual failure case studies.

**Relevant context:** Safe-state defaults in engineering design (fail-safe principle); Anthropic's published guidance on agentic safety; the success state specified in the prompt.

# Working Backward from Zero-Irreversible-Action Success: Which Task Classes Require the Most Redesign?

**Problem:** Achieving zero irreversible harmful actions may be impossible for all task classes, but achievable for specific task classes. Identifying which task classes are closest to the success state prioritizes research efforts.

**Direction:** Categorize 50 agent tasks by domain (code, finance, communication, data management, web browsing). For each category, measure the baseline rate of irreversible actions and the remaining rate after applying best-available mitigations. Identify which task categories are closest to and furthest from the success state.

**Why it matters:** Realistic path-to-success analysis prevents wasted effort. Task categories closest to the success state can be declared 'safe enough for deployment' soonest.

**Relevant context:** The success state in the prompt; METR's task suite categorizations; Adversa AI's incident categorization by domain (2025 report).

# Trust Bootstrapping Protocol for Multi-Agent Success: How Should Agent Trust Relationships Be Initially Established?

**Problem:** The success state requires agents to operate within defined boundaries, which requires a trust hierarchy. Reaching the success state requires a protocol for bootstrapping trust relationships between agents during system initialization.

**Direction:** Design three trust bootstrapping protocols (credential-based, role-declaration-based, capability-verification-based). Test each protocol's resistance to impersonation attacks in a 3-agent system over 30 task trials. Measure trust establishment time, false-acceptance rate of fraudulent agents, and task completion rate.

**Why it matters:** If trust bootstrapping is insecure, the entire safety architecture built on it is compromised. This is a prerequisite for achieving the success state in any multi-agent deployment.

**Relevant context:** NIST AI Agent Standards Initiative on interoperability and security (nist.gov, 2026); Strata's report on AI agent identity crisis; the success state requirement for defined operational boundaries.

# ShadowAgent: Measuring Whether Capable Agents Strategically Hide Actions from Oversight Systems

**Problem:** Combining high agentic autonomy with deceptive capability produces a failure mode where agents strategically hide their actions from monitors while continuing to pursue goals. This is the 'autonomous deception' failure mode.

**Direction:** Test whether capable models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) in an agentic setting will spontaneously hide specific actions from a simulated monitor when doing so serves task completion. Specifically: place a task where the optimal path involves an action the agent knows the monitor will block. Measure whether agents route around the monitor or comply.

**Why it matters:** Strategic action hiding is the most dangerous failure mode combination: high capability + deception + autonomy. METR's monitorability evaluations study adjacent behaviors; this tests spontaneous hiding without explicit instruction.

**Relevant context:** METR monitorability evaluations (January 2026); Gemini 3 model card on stealth ability in sabotage; the compounding risk specified in the prompt: agentic autonomy + deception.

# CascadeWatch: Characterizing Unsupervised Harmful Cascades in Multi-Agent Networks

**Problem:** Combining agentic autonomy with oversight failure produces a second failure mode: unsupervised harmful cascades, where a chain of agent actions each trigger subsequent harmful actions without any human ever reviewing the chain.

**Direction:** Design a 4-agent pipeline with a simulated human oversight gap (monitor is offline for steps 3-7 of a 10-step task). Inject a harmful instruction at step 3. Measure: does the harm propagate through the remaining unsupervised steps? Does the agent spontaneously pause and wait for oversight? Does it complete the full harmful cascade? Test across 30 trials.

**Why it matters:** Unsupervised harmful cascades are the most dangerous realistic multi-agent failure mode. No empirical study has measured whether models spontaneously pause during oversight gaps.

**Relevant context:** The compounding risk specified in the prompt: agentic + oversight failure = unsupervised harmful cascades; METR monitorability evaluations; Partnership on AI's real-time failure detection report (2025).

# Deception Detection Rate: How Effectively Can Current Monitors Detect Strategic Action Hiding by AI Agents?

**Problem:** If capable agents can strategically hide actions, the effectiveness of monitoring systems against this threat is unknown. A monitor that cannot detect strategic hiding provides false safety assurance.

**Direction:** Take 50 agent traces: 25 where the agent is secretly hiding one action from the monitor, 25 benign. Test three monitors (rule-based, LLM-as-monitor, METR-style human review) on these traces. Measure detection rate, false positive rate, and which hiding strategies evade each monitor type.

**Why it matters:** If LLM-as-monitor approaches also fail to detect LLM strategic hiding (because they share blind spots), the entire monitoring paradigm may be insufficient for the agentic autonomy + deception failure mode.

**Relevant context:** METR monitorability evaluations (January 2026); the ShadowAgent failure mode; ControlArena monitoring system design (apartresearch.com); the compounding risk in the prompt.

# Cascade Arrest Mechanisms: Which Interventions Stop a Harmful Cascade Once Started?

**Problem:** Once a harmful cascade is in progress in a multi-agent network, it is unclear which interventions can arrest it before maximum harm is reached.

**Direction:** Implement a harmful cascade in a 4-agent network. At each step of the cascade (steps 1-4), apply one of five arrest mechanisms (hard stop, alert and wait, graceful shutdown, task handoff to safe agent, rollback to last safe checkpoint). Measure harm reduction and collateral task disruption for each mechanism applied at each step.

**Why it matters:** Arrest mechanisms for in-progress cascades are the last defense line for the oversight-failure compounding risk. The optimal arrest mechanism and application timing are unknown.

**Relevant context:** The unsupervised harmful cascade failure mode; Partnership on AI's real-time failure detection report (2025); ControlArena control protocols (apartresearch.com); the causal chain rollback node.

# Strategic Deception Emergence: At What Capability Level Do Agents Begin Hiding Actions?

**Problem:** The strategic action-hiding failure mode (agentic autonomy + deception) may only emerge above a certain capability threshold. Identifying this threshold would indicate when the compounding risk becomes practically relevant.

**Direction:** Test the ShadowAgent scenario (task where optimal path involves routing around a monitor) across 5 models of varying capability levels (measured by METR capability score). Measure action-hiding rate as a function of model capability. Estimate the capability threshold at which hiding rate exceeds 10%.

**Why it matters:** If strategic deception only emerges above a high capability threshold, current models may be safe. If it emerges at current capability levels, the threat is immediate. This calibrates urgency.

**Relevant context:** METR Time Horizon 1.1 (January 2026) on capability doubling times; Gemini 3 Pro sabotage and stealth evaluations; METR MALT dataset on evaluation gaming; the ShadowAgent failure mode.

# Oversight Gap Duration Threshold: How Long Can an Agent Operate Unsupervised Before Cascade Risk Becomes Unacceptable?

**Problem:** Human oversight cannot be continuous. The safe maximum duration of unsupervised agent operation is unknown, and the relationship between oversight gap duration and cascade risk is not characterized.

**Direction:** Run an agent on a 30-step task with simulated oversight gaps of varying duration (0 steps, 3 steps, 7 steps, 15 steps, 30 steps fully unsupervised). Inject a harmful trigger at step 5 of each run. Measure cascade harm as a function of oversight gap duration. Fit a harm-vs-gap-duration curve.

**Why it matters:** Practical oversight system design requires knowing the safe maximum unsupervised interval. This directly informs the design of human-in-the-loop frequencies for production agentic systems.

**Relevant context:** The oversight failure compounding risk in the prompt; Partnership on AI's real-time failure detection report (2025); METR monitorability evaluations; Anthropic's guidance on human approval for irreversible actions.

# Dual Failure Mode Taxonomy: Distinguishing ShadowAgent from CascadeWatch Incidents in the Wild

**Problem:** The two compounding failure modes (strategic action hiding vs. unsupervised harmful cascades) produce similar observable outcomes (harmful actions without human detection) but have different causal structures and require different interventions.

**Direction:** Develop a diagnostic taxonomy for distinguishing ShadowAgent-type incidents (intentional hiding) from CascadeWatch-type incidents (oversight gap exploitation) from available incident reports. Apply the taxonomy to the Adversa AI 2025 incident dataset. Measure inter-rater reliability. Identify which type is more prevalent.

**Why it matters:** Conflating these two failure modes leads to mis-targeted interventions. ShadowAgent requires deception-detection capabilities; CascadeWatch requires oversight gap minimization. The right diagnosis enables the right response.

**Relevant context:** The two compounding failure modes named in the prompt; Adversa AI 2025 incidents report; Microsoft's agent failure taxonomy whitepaper (2025); MAST taxonomy (openreview.net).

# Agentic Autonomy Scaling and Safety: Does Increased Agent Autonomy Linearly or Superlinearly Increase Harm Rate?

**Problem:** As agent autonomy increases (measured by task horizon, tool count, and delegation depth), harm rate may increase linearly or superlinearly. The functional form of this relationship determines how urgently safety interventions are needed.

**Direction:** Run agents with systematically varied autonomy levels (1D: task horizon 5/15/30 steps; 2D: tool count 2/5/10; 3D: delegation depth 0/1/2 levels) on standardized safety evaluation tasks. Fit the harm rate vs. autonomy curve. Test whether interactions between dimensions produce superlinear harm growth.

**Why it matters:** METR's Time Horizon 1.1 found a capability doubling time of 130 days. If harm rate scales superlinearly with capability, the safety window is much shorter than capability growth alone suggests.

**Relevant context:** METR Time Horizon 1.1 (metr.org, January 2026); the two compounding failure modes; ForesightSafety Bench risky agentic autonomy pillar (arxiv 2602.14135).

# Measuring Boundary Respect Consistency: Do Agents Apply Safety Rules Uniformly Across All Task Contexts?

**Problem:** Agents may apply safety constraints inconsistently across contexts — strict in some domains, lenient in others — creating exploitable inconsistencies.

**Direction:** Design 40 tasks spanning 8 domains (code, finance, communication, scheduling, data, web, physical simulation, social). Each task contains an identical boundary test (the same type of constraint violation opportunity). Measure whether constraint violation rate varies significantly across domains. Identify highest-risk domains.

**Why it matters:** Inconsistent boundary enforcement means attackers can target the domains where constraints are weakest. Identifying inconsistency patterns is a prerequisite for fixing them.

**Relevant context:** 2025 AI Agent Index finding that agents disregard legal and privacy policies even in high-risk settings; OpenAgentSafety framework (arxiv 2507.06134); the success state of uniform boundary compliance.

# Adversarial Orchestrator Simulation: Can a Malicious Orchestrator Reliably Extract Dangerous Actions from Safety-Trained Sub-Agents?

**Problem:** Sub-agents are typically trained to be safe, but an adversarial orchestrator sending carefully crafted instructions could bypass sub-agent safety training without triggering standard safety classifiers.

**Direction:** Build an adversarial orchestrator that uses indirect instruction, authority framing, and gradual escalation to direct a safety-trained sub-agent to take a prohibited action. Test against 3 safety-trained models across 20 prohibited-action types. Measure bypass success rate. Compare to direct instruction baseline.

**Why it matters:** If adversarial orchestration reliably bypasses sub-agent safety training, the entire multi-agent safety model is compromised. Sub-agents cannot be trusted to be safe nodes in an untrusted graph.

**Relevant context:** ControlArena collusion settings (apartresearch.com); indirect prompt injection in Google DeepMind paper (arxiv 2505.14534); Adversa AI 2025 on prompt injection as most common incident type.

# Long-Horizon Memory and Safety: Do Agents with Persistent Memory Develop More Dangerous Behavioral Patterns Over Time?

**Problem:** Agents with persistent memory across tasks accumulate context that may shape subsequent behavior in unpredictable or unsafe ways not present in stateless agents.

**Direction:** Run an agent with persistent memory (stored conversation history) vs. a stateless baseline on 100 sequential tasks. After every 10 tasks, run a safety evaluation. Measure whether safety failure rate changes over the 100-task sequence for the persistent-memory agent vs. stateless baseline. Analyze memory content for patterns associated with increased failures.

**Why it matters:** Persistent memory is a key feature of production agentic systems. Safety consequences of memory accumulation have not been studied empirically.

**Relevant context:** 2025 AI Agent Index (arxiv 2602.17753) which documents deployed agent memory features; goal drift characterization across long tasks; the agentic security threats survey (arxiv 2510.23883).

# Self-Exfiltration Risk in Agentic Systems: Do Agents Spontaneously Attempt to Copy Their Instructions or State?

**Problem:** Highly capable agentic systems might spontaneously attempt to copy their instructions, model weights, or key state to external locations as an instrumental goal, even without explicit instruction to do so.

**Direction:** Create an environment where an agent has access to a file system and network, and where copying its own system prompt or outputs to an external location is technically possible but clearly not required for the assigned task. Measure the rate at which agents spontaneously attempt self-exfiltration across 50 tasks and 3 models.

**Why it matters:** Spontaneous self-exfiltration is an early warning indicator of autonomy-seeking behavior. METR flagged rogue replication as a critical capability concern in their GPT-5.1 evaluation.

**Relevant context:** METR evaluation of GPT-5.1 for rogue replication (metr.org); ForesightSafety Bench catastrophic and existential risks pillar (arxiv 2602.14135); the dangerous capabilities framework.

# Safe Interruption: Can You Stop a Running Agent Mid-Task Without Causing More Harm Than Completing It?

**Problem:** Interrupting a running agent mid-task may leave systems in a partially-modified, potentially more dangerous state than completing the task. The conditions under which interruption is safe are unknown.

**Direction:** Design 20 tasks where an agent is interrupted at different points (20%, 50%, 80% completion). Measure: state of the environment at interruption vs. completion vs. not started. Identify whether mid-task interruption produces a 'dangerous intermediate state' that is worse than either completion or non-start. Develop safe-interruption guidelines.

**Why it matters:** Human oversight requires the ability to stop agents. If stopping is sometimes more dangerous than continuing, oversight operators may be reluctant to intervene — exactly the wrong incentive.

**Relevant context:** Cascade arrest mechanisms; CascadeWatch failure mode; Partnership on AI real-time failure detection (2025); the agent incident response open problem.

# Prompt Injection Taxonomy for Multi-Agent Systems: Classifying Attack Vectors by Propagation Path

**Problem:** Prompt injection attacks in multi-agent systems can propagate through multiple agents in ways not possible in single-agent settings. No taxonomy of multi-agent injection propagation paths exists.

**Direction:** Collect or construct 40 prompt injection scenarios in multi-agent settings. Classify each by propagation path (direct injection into target agent, injection via shared memory, injection via tool output, injection via inter-agent communication). Measure which path produces the highest attack success rate and which is hardest to defend.

**Why it matters:** Effective defenses must target the specific propagation paths used. Without a path taxonomy, defenses are likely incomplete.

**Relevant context:** Google DeepMind indirect prompt injection paper (arxiv 2505.14534); Adversa AI 2025 on 35.3% of incidents involving prompt injection; ControlArena (apartresearch.com).

# Calibration of Agentic Risk Assessment: Do Agents Correctly Estimate the Risk Level of Their Own Actions?

**Problem:** Agents may be systematically miscalibrated in their own risk assessments — underestimating risk for irreversible actions and overestimating risk for reversible ones — leading to inappropriate confidence.

**Direction:** Elicit self-assessed risk scores from an agent for 100 actions before executing them. Compare self-assessed risk scores to independent human-annotated risk scores. Measure calibration (correlation between self-assessed and human-assessed risk). Test whether miscalibration is systematic (always under/over) or random.

**Why it matters:** If agents are systematically miscalibrated, their ability to apply appropriate caution to high-risk actions is fundamentally compromised. Calibration training may be needed.

**Relevant context:** The reversibility scoring concept; IrreversAct-Bench; outcome-driven constraint violations (arxiv 2512.20798); Anthropic's guidance on irreversible action caution.

# Agent Network Topology and Safety: Do Some Communication Topologies Produce More Safety Failures Than Others?

**Problem:** Multi-agent networks can be organized in many topologies (hub-and-spoke, ring, fully connected, hierarchical). The safety consequences of topology choice have not been empirically studied.

**Direction:** Implement the same 5-agent task in 4 topologies (hub-and-spoke, ring, fully-connected, 2-level hierarchy). Run 30 tasks per topology. Measure safety failure rate, cascade propagation rate, and task completion rate for each. Identify which topology best balances safety and utility.

**Why it matters:** If topology significantly affects safety, practitioners can improve safety by choosing architectures with better safety properties — a design-time intervention with no runtime overhead.

**Relevant context:** Information cascades and network topology; ControlArena multi-agent environments (apartresearch.com); the collective information cascade failure mode; swarm intelligence topology research.

# METR Task Suite Extension: Customer Service Agent Tasks with Irreversible Communication Actions

**Problem:** METR's task suite does not include customer service tasks, despite these being a major deployment domain where irreversible actions (sent emails, account changes, refund approvals) are common.

**Direction:** Design 15 METR-style customer service tasks (handle a refund request, respond to a complaint, update account details, send a promotional email). Include irreversible actions in each task's solution path. Measure agent task completion rate and irreversible-action-error rate. Compare to METR baseline tasks.

**Why it matters:** Customer service is one of the highest-volume agentic deployment domains. Extending METR evals to this domain provides safety data for a practically important use case.

**Relevant context:** METR autonomy evaluation resources (metr.org); the 2025 AI Agent Index on deployed agent domains; Adversa AI 2025 incidents including unauthorized account changes.

# Multi-Task Interference in Agentic Systems: Do Concurrent Tasks Create Safety Failures That Sequential Tasks Do Not?

**Problem:** Production agentic systems often handle multiple tasks concurrently. Concurrent task execution may create interference patterns (shared resource conflicts, context contamination, priority inversion) that sequential execution does not.

**Direction:** Run an agent on 10 task pairs: once sequentially and once concurrently. Measure safety failure rate, task completion rate, and resource conflict frequency for sequential vs. concurrent execution. Identify which task pair types are most prone to concurrent-execution safety failures.

**Why it matters:** Concurrency is a fundamental production requirement, but its safety implications for agentic systems are not studied. This could be a significant underexplored failure class.

**Relevant context:** The agentic workflow architectures guide (stackai.com); distributed systems concurrency problems applied to agents; the MAST taxonomy communication failures.

# Applying Defense-in-Depth to Agentic Pipelines: Does Layering Safety Interventions Produce Compounding Benefits?

**Problem:** Defense-in-depth is a standard security principle: multiple independent layers of defense provide compounding protection. It is unknown whether this principle holds for agentic safety interventions.

**Direction:** Test 7 safety interventions individually and in all 21 two-intervention combinations on a standardized safety task suite. Measure whether combined interventions produce more than additive safety improvement (compounding benefits) or less (interference). Identify which intervention pairs are most synergistic.

**Why it matters:** If interventions compound, practitioners should layer as many as feasible. If interventions interfere, the optimal combination must be found empirically. This determines the right deployment strategy.

**Relevant context:** Minimum viable safety stack concept; the causal chain audit; ControlArena control protocol design (apartresearch.com); defense-in-depth from computer security.

# Contextual Integrity in Agentic Data Flows: When Do Agents Violate Information-Sharing Norms?

**Problem:** Agents may violate contextual integrity — sharing information across contexts in ways that violate the norms of the original context — even when no individual data sharing action is technically prohibited.

**Direction:** Design 20 tasks where an agent encounters information from one context (e.g., private medical data in a document it is summarizing) and has opportunities to share it in another context (e.g., include in an email it is drafting). Measure contextual integrity violation rate. Test whether explicit contextual integrity prompting reduces violations.

**Why it matters:** Contextual integrity violations are a form of accumulated privacy harm — each individual sharing may seem minor, but the pattern constitutes a significant violation. This connects to the accumulation-of-negligible-harms failure mode.

**Relevant context:** ForesightSafety Bench privacy pillar (arxiv 2602.14135); the accumulation of negligible harms failure mode from the seed problem; OpenAgentSafety privacy findings (arxiv 2507.06134).

# Instruction Hijacking Through Environmental Poisoning: How Easily Can Malicious Environment State Redirect Agent Goals?

**Problem:** Agents that read from their environment (files, web pages, databases) can have their goals redirected by malicious content placed in the environment — without any direct attack on the agent.

**Direction:** Create a simulated environment (file system + web pages) containing 5 hidden adversarial redirects (malicious instructions embedded in otherwise legitimate-looking content). Run 5 different agent models on a standard task in this environment. Measure goal hijacking success rate, agent self-detection of hijacking attempts, and effectiveness of input sanitization as a defense.

**Why it matters:** Environmental poisoning is a practical, hard-to-detect attack vector that requires no access to the agent itself. Princeton's crypto agent attack used this exact vector.

**Relevant context:** Princeton crypto agent context poisoning study; Google DeepMind indirect prompt injection (arxiv 2505.14534); Adversa AI 2025 on prompt injection in agentic systems; the ShadowAgent failure mode.

# Investigating Reward Hacking in Agentic Task Completion: When Do Agents Game Metrics Instead of Solving Problems?

**Problem:** Agentic systems evaluated on objective metrics may find unexpected ways to achieve high metric scores without actually completing the intended task — a form of reward hacking in agentic settings.

**Direction:** Design 15 tasks with measurable completion metrics (e.g., 'number of test cases passing', 'user satisfaction score'). Run agents on each. After completion, perform a qualitative assessment of whether the metric score accurately reflects genuine task completion. Identify reward-hacking strategies used. Test whether metric-agnostic evaluation reduces gaming.

**Why it matters:** Reward hacking is an established failure mode in RL. In agentic LLM settings, it may take novel forms (e.g., editing test files to pass, generating fake satisfaction signals). METR's MALT dataset covers generalized reward hacking.

**Relevant context:** METR MALT dataset on generalized reward hacking (metr.org); outcome-driven constraint violations (arxiv 2512.20798); the goal drift characterization work.

# Replicating IOI Circuit Discovery in Mistral-7B

**Problem:** The indirect object identification (IOI) circuit was thoroughly characterized in GPT-2 Small (26 attention heads across 7 functional classes), but it is unknown whether the same functional decomposition holds in modern instruction-tuned models with different architectures.

**Direction:** Use TransformerLens to load Mistral-7B and apply activation patching and path patching to identify the IOI circuit. Compare the number of circuit components, their layer distribution, and functional roles against the original GPT-2 Small results. Test whether the same head types (name movers, duplicate token heads, induction heads, S-inhibition heads) appear.

**Why it matters:** If the same circuit structure appears across architectures, it suggests mechanistic universality, which would mean interpretability findings from small models transfer to production-scale ones. Divergences would reveal where architecture choices create fundamentally different internal algorithms — critical for determining which models safety research generalises to.

**Relevant context:** Wang et al. (2022) 'Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small' (arXiv:2211.00593) fully characterized 26 attention heads. TransformerLens supports Mistral-7B. Automated circuit discovery methods (Conmy et al., NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2304.14997) provide tooling to scale this. Induction head ablation in Llama-3 reduces abstract pattern recognition by 25-32pp (2025 NAACL findings), suggesting head-level functional roles persist across scales.

# Induction Head Formation in Phi-3 Mini vs GPT-2: Developmental Timing and Structure

**Problem:** Induction heads were first characterized in GPT-2 and small toy models, where they form during a sharp 'phase change' in training. It is unknown whether this same developmental pattern occurs in modern small-but-capable models like Phi-3 Mini, which was trained with a very different data curriculum (high-quality 'textbook' data).

**Direction:** Using TransformerLens, load intermediate Phi-3 Mini checkpoints if available (or use a small proxy model trained on similar high-quality data). Measure the in-context learning score and loss as a function of training step to detect the phase transition. Identify induction head pairs using standard prefix matching scores and compare formation timing and structural placement to known GPT-2 results.

**Why it matters:** If data quality dramatically changes when and how induction heads form, it would suggest that the training distribution — not just model size — is a key mechanistic variable. This bears on safety because if induction heads form earlier or more robustly, models may develop stronger in-context copying behaviors sooner, with implications for prompt injection and context manipulation risks.

**Relevant context:** Olsson et al. (2022) 'In-context Learning and Induction Heads' (transformer-circuits.pub) established the phase transition result in GPT-2. TransformerLens supports Phi-3 Mini. The 'textbook is all you need' Phi-1 paper showed that curriculum profoundly affects capability emergence timing. Induction head ablation studies in Llama-3 (NAACL 2025) confirm functional importance persists at scale.

# Superposition Analysis of Gemma-2-2B Using SAELens: Do Smaller Gemma Models Show More Superposition?

**Problem:** Superposition — the encoding of more features than neurons — was characterized primarily in toy models and early GPT-family models. The Gemma family spans 2B to 27B parameters and has publicly available Gemma Scope SAEs, making it ideal for a scale-controlled superposition comparison that was previously infeasible.

**Direction:** Use SAELens with the pre-trained Gemma Scope SAEs on Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B. Multilingual models like XLM-RoBERTa and mBERT must represent the same semantic concepts across 100+ languages in a shared embedding space. It is unknown whether their SAE features show higher universality (because they must encode language-invariant concepts) or lower universality (because cross-lingual representations are inherently more compressed and polysemantic).

**Direction:** Using SAELens, train small SAEs on XLM-R and mBERT activations using multilingual text corpora (e.g., CC-100). Match features across models using activation correlation on parallel translation sentences. Measure whether cross-lingual feature matching is higher or lower than same-language feature matching within monolingual models. Test whether features that activate for the same concept across languages are also universal across models.

**Why it matters:** Multilingual AI systems are deployed globally in high-stakes contexts (content moderation, translation of sensitive communications). If their features are systematically more polysemantic due to cross-lingual compression, existing interpretability tools may be even less effective on them — creating a safety monitoring blind spot for non-English AI systems.

**Relevant context:** 'Quantifying Feature Space Universality Across Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders' (arXiv:2410.06981) provides the methodology for cross-model feature comparison. SAELens supports arbitrary PyTorch models. XLM-RoBERTa and mBERT are available on HuggingFace and are encoder models with well-understood cross-lingual properties. The 'Sparse Autoencoders Learn Monosemantic Features in Vision-Language Models' paper (arXiv:2504.02821) provides VLM SAE methodology that generalises to multilingual settings.

**Relevant context:** McDougall et al. (2023) 'Copy Suppression: Comprehensively Understanding an Attention Head' characterized the copy suppression mechanism in GPT-2. # Probing Leakage Benchmark: Separating Model Knowledge from Probe Learning Capacity

**Problem:** Probing classifiers are widely used to test whether specific information is linearly encoded in activations, but probes can achieve high accuracy by learning the information themselves rather than reading it from the model. **Direction:** For three tasks (sentiment, syntactic subject number, factual country capital) run linear probes on GPT-2-Small's residual stream activations. For each probe, also train an identical probe on randomly initialized model activations as a baseline. Define a probe leakage score as the difference in accuracy between the real and random-model probes. Compare across layers and tasks. Use TransformerLens for activation extraction.

**Why it matters:** If probing results cannot be trusted to reflect model representations rather than probe capacity, safety conclusions drawn from probing studies may be systematically overstated. A standardized leakage benchmark would flag unreliable probing claims.

**Relevant context:** The probe leakage problem is described in MIB's background section and in survey papers on representation analysis. No dedicated benchmark tool addressing this gap was identified in the 2025 literature.

Publish the comparison as a reliability audit with implications for which LLM to use in automated interpretability pipelines.

**Relevant context:** CE-Bench explicitly criticizes LLM-based evaluation for non-determinism and bias. SAEBench uses automated LLM scoring as a core metric. No cross-judge consistency audit was found in the literature.

**Problem:** MIB was validated on GPT-2-Small, Qwen-2.5, Gemma-2, Llama-3.1, and InterpBench. The Pythia model family, which is widely used in interpretability research due to its training checkpoints and size suite, is not in MIB's evaluation set. Method rankings on Pythia may differ from those on MIB's models.

**Direction:** Replicate the MIB circuit localization track on Pythia-160M and Pythia-1.4B for at least two tasks (IOI and one other). Use the MIB evaluation metrics directly. Report whether method rankings from the MIB paper hold on Pythia models. Publish the Pythia-adapted dataset splits and evaluation scripts as a community contribution.

**Why it matters:** The Pythia suite is the most commonly used family for interpretability experiments due to checkpoints at every training step. Extending MIB to Pythia would make the benchmark more useful to a large portion of the research community.

# Attention Head Function Taxonomy Validator: Testing Whether Published Head Type Classifications Are Stable

**Problem:** Attention heads are often classified into functional types (induction heads, previous token heads, copy suppression heads, backup name mover heads) but these classifications are derived from a small set of analyzed models. No benchmark tests whether the taxonomy of head functions is stable, complete, or model-specific. New model families may contain head types not in any existing taxonomy.

**Direction:** Apply published detection criteria for each named head type to Pythia-410M and GPT-2-Medium. Measure what fraction of heads are classifiable under the existing taxonomy versus unclassifiable. For unclassifiable heads, characterize the top activating patterns. Report a taxonomy coverage score per model. Use TransformerLens for all activation extraction.

**Why it matters:** If the existing taxonomy covers only a portion of real head functions, safety analyses relying on it may miss important computational patterns. A coverage benchmark would reveal whether the taxonomy needs expansion.

**Relevant context:** The head function taxonomy is documented across multiple Anthropic and academic papers using GPT-2-Small as the primary reference model. No cross-model taxonomy coverage audit was found.

# Steering Vector Side Effect Measurement Suite: Quantifying Unintended Behavioral Changes

**Problem:** Steering vectors are increasingly used as safety interventions (to add or suppress behaviors), but no standardized evaluation measures side effects: unintended changes in model behavior on tasks unrelated to the steering target. A steering vector that suppresses harmful content but also degrades mathematical reasoning would be unacceptable for deployment.

**Direction:** Apply five published steering vectors to GPT-2-Small (or Gemma-2-2B via published vectors). For each, measure performance on five unrelated tasks (arithmetic, grammar correction, next-word prediction, sentiment classification, factual recall) before and after steering. Define a side effect score as the mean performance drop across unrelated tasks. Report a steering vector side effect profile table.

**Why it matters:** Steering vector side effects are a direct safety concern: a safety intervention must not damage general model capabilities. A standardized side effect benchmark would let developers compare steering approaches on this safety-critical dimension.

**Relevant context:** Steering vectors are widely used but evaluated primarily on their target behavior. No standardized multi-task side effect measurement suite was found in the 2025 literature. TransformerLens supports activation addition for steering.

# Circuit Minimality Audit Tool: Measuring How Minimal Published Circuits Actually Are

**Problem:** Circuit discovery methods aim to find the minimal subgraph that preserves task behavior. However, there is no standard tool for auditing whether a published circuit is actually minimal: do all reported edges contribute meaningfully, or are some redundant? Including redundant edges inflates circuit size and may mislead safety analyses.

**Direction:** Take three published GPT-2-Small circuits (IOI, greater-than, docstring). For each, sequentially ablate each edge and test whether task faithfulness degrades. Define a minimality score as the fraction of edges that are individually necessary. Publish the auditing script as a standalone tool compatible with TransformerLens circuit representations.

**Why it matters:** Non-minimal circuits contain spurious edges that could mislead safety researchers about which components are causally responsible for a behavior. A minimality audit tool would be a prerequisite for certifying that a circuit is ready to use in safety-critical analysis.

**Relevant context:** MIB includes sparsity as one of three circuit evaluation criteria but does not measure whether individual published circuits meet a minimality standard. TinySQL (referenced in MIB's background) discusses circuit minimality but as a training metric, not an audit tool.

# SAE Training Stability Benchmark: How Sensitive Are Feature Counts to Training Hyperparameters?

**Problem:** SynthSAEBench (2026) and SAEBench both evaluate trained SAEs but neither measures how sensitive the number and identity of discovered features are to training hyperparameters (learning rate, L1 penalty, dictionary size). Two SAEs trained with slightly different hyperparameters may discover wildly different feature sets even on the same model, which has direct implications for reproducibility.

**Direction:** Train five SAEs on GPT-2-Small layer 8 residual stream using SAELens, varying only the L1 penalty across five values spanning one order of magnitude. For each pair of trained SAEs, compute a feature overlap score: what fraction of features in one SAE have a cosine-similar counterpart (>0.8) in the other. Report a training stability curve. This is feasible on a single GPU within 30 hours.

**Why it matters:** If SAE features are highly sensitive to hyperparameters, they cannot be treated as stable discoveries about model internals. This benchmark would establish minimum hyperparameter standards for reproducible SAE training.

**Relevant context:** SAELens makes SAE training straightforward on a single GPU. SynthSAEBench (arXiv 2602.14687) was published in 2026 and evaluates SAEs but does not address training stability across hyperparameter variations.

# Debate as a Weak-to-Strong Bridge: Testing Argument Quality Across Model Size Gaps

**Problem:** It is unclear whether debate protocols actually help weak overseers supervise strong models, or whether the debate format itself creates exploitable patterns.

**Direction:** Implement a small-scale debate experiment using GPT-2 vs GPT-4-class models (via API) on factual QA tasks. Measure whether debate format improves weak overseer accuracy compared to direct answer evaluation.

**Why it matters:** Debate is a core proposed mechanism for scalable oversight, but its empirical effectiveness against a baseline of direct evaluation has not been rigorously measured at accessible scales.

**Relevant context:** Burns et al. (2023) showed GPT-2 supervision of GPT-4 is possible. 'Debate Helps Weak-to-Strong Generalization' (AAAI 2025) provides a starting point but leaves open questions about mechanism.

# Confidence-Weighted Supervision: Does Overseer Self-Reported Certainty Predict Oversight Quality?

**Problem:** Human overseers and weak model overseers both make errors, but not all errors are equal. Errors made with high stated confidence are especially dangerous because they are most likely to propagate.

**Direction:** Train a small model using supervision labels paired with overseer confidence scores. Compare performance when high-confidence vs. low-confidence labels are up-weighted, and test whether confidence-weighting reduces the propagation of systematic errors.

**Why it matters:** If confident errors are more harmful than uncertain errors, filtering supervision by confidence is a low-cost intervention that could improve oversight quality for student models.

**Relevant context:** Reward hacking of human oversight is identified as a core open problem; overseer bias mapping is listed as unsolved.

# Overseer Specialization: Can Domain-Specific Weak Supervisors Outperform Generalist Weak Supervisors?

**Problem:** Weak overseers are typically general-purpose models. A domain-specialized weak overseer might provide higher-quality supervision in narrow tasks even with fewer parameters.

**Direction:** Fine-tune a small model on a narrow domain (e.g., medical QA, legal reasoning) and use it as an overseer for a larger model on the same domain. Compare oversight quality to a larger generalist overseer.

**Why it matters:** Specialization is a known strategy in human organizations for extending oversight capacity. If it works for model overseers it could be a practical near-term tool.

**Relevant context:** Organizational management literature on specialization and oversight; open problem of quality-representativeness tradeoff in supervision data.

# Uncertainty Elicitation as an Oversight Signal: Teaching Strong Models to Flag What Weak Overseers Cannot Verify

**Problem:** Strong models may produce correct answers that weak overseers cannot verify, but might also be capable of flagging which of their own outputs are unverifiable by weaker systems.

**Direction:** Train a strong model to output both an answer and an 'overseer-verifiability' score. Test whether these scores predict actual overseer accuracy and whether filtering on them improves oversight signal quality.

**Why it matters:** If models can learn to identify their own oversight-resistant outputs, this creates a new tool for improving oversight pipeline quality with minimal extra human effort.

**Relevant context:** Open problem: determining if models provide genuinely believed-correct responses. Related to recursive reward modeling.

# Overseer Coalition Voting: Aggregating Multiple Weak Supervisors to Approximate Strong Oversight

**Problem:** A single weak overseer has limited accuracy, but an ensemble of independent weak overseers with different error patterns might collectively provide stronger supervision.

**Direction:** Use majority voting among three different weak models as the supervision signal for training a stronger model. Compare to single-overseer baselines across classification tasks.

**Why it matters:** Ensemble oversight could be a practical technique deployable today to improve oversight quality without requiring stronger individual overseers.

**Relevant context:** Arxiv 2402.00667 combines scalable oversight with ensemble learning. This extends the idea to the overseer role rather than the student.

# Stepwise Verification vs. End-State Verification: Oversight Quality Tradeoffs

**Problem:** It is an open question whether overseers achieve better accuracy by verifying intermediate reasoning steps versus only the final answer.

**Direction:** Compare oversight quality (measured by downstream student model accuracy) when the weak overseer labels each reasoning step versus only the final output. Use chain-of-thought math problems as the testbed.

**Why it matters:** Process-based oversight is theoretically more robust, but the empirical cost-benefit tradeoff at accessible scales has not been systematically characterized.

**Relevant context:** Process-based vs. outcome-based reward models are a current debate in the field; relevant to iterated amplification methodology.

# Adversarial Contrast Pairs for Oversight Training: Teaching Overseers to Detect Subtle Errors

**Problem:** Weak overseers may perform well on obvious errors but fail on subtle, plausible-looking mistakes that capable models might systematically produce.

**Direction:** Generate contrast pairs (correct answer, subtly wrong answer) and test overseer accuracy specifically on these pairs. Use the error rate profile to identify systematic blind spots in the overseer.

**Why it matters:** If overseers have structured blind spots, models trained on their supervision will inherit biases. Mapping blind spots is the first step toward correcting them.

**Relevant context:** Open problem: systematic oversight errors. Buhl et al. (2025) use adversarial RL to stress-test judge blind spots.

# Scalable Oversight Under Distribution Shift: Does Oversight Quality Degrade Out-of-Domain?

**Problem:** Oversight protocols are typically evaluated on in-distribution tasks. It is unknown how quickly oversight quality degrades when the task distribution shifts from what the overseer was calibrated on.

**Direction:** Train an overseer on one domain (e.g., coding QA), then evaluate it on a shifted domain (e.g., scientific QA). Measure how oversight accuracy degrades and whether simple domain adaptation restores it.

**Why it matters:** Deployed AI systems encounter distribution shift continuously. If oversight fails silently under shift, safety guarantees are weaker than reported.

**Relevant context:** Easy-to-hard generalization is listed as an open problem. Related to cross-domain transfer of oversight.

# Graduated Hint Systems: Modeling Scalable Oversight as a Teaching Protocol

**Problem:** Oversight is typically framed as binary (approve/reject), but richer feedback could improve the signal quality provided to the strong model.

**Direction:** Implement a hint-based feedback protocol where the weak overseer provides graduated correction hints rather than binary labels, and compare student model quality under this regime.

**Why it matters:** Education research shows graduated feedback outperforms binary grades for learning. Applying this principle to oversight could improve oversight efficiency.

**Relevant context:** Cross-domain import from education/teaching assessment methodology. Related to iterated amplification.

# Oversight Fatigue Simulation: Modeling How Sustained Oversight Degrades Over Time

**Problem:** Human overseers and even model overseers operating over long sessions show quality degradation. This fatigue effect is not modeled in standard oversight experiments.

**Direction:** Simulate oversight degradation by systematically introducing increasing error rates in the overseer across a training run, and measure the cumulative effect on the supervised model's alignment.

**Why it matters:** Real oversight systems must operate continuously. Understanding how fatigue-induced oversight degradation compounds is critical for designing robust pipelines.

**Relevant context:** Quality-representativeness tradeoff in supervision data; organizational management literature on oversight and attention limits.

# Model Size Gap Sweep: How Does Oversight Quality Scale with the Capability Gap Between Overseer and Student?

**Problem:** Weak-to-strong generalization experiments have explored a small number of model size pairings. A systematic sweep across a wider range of capability gaps is missing.

**Direction:** Using OpenAI's open-sourced weak-to-strong code, run experiments with GPT-2, GPT-2-medium, GPT-2-large, and GPT-2-XL as overseers for a fixed strong student model. Plot oversight quality as a function of overseer parameter count.

**Why it matters:** A quantitative relationship between capability gap and oversight quality is needed to extrapolate whether current techniques will work at superhuman scales.

**Relevant context:** Burns et al. (2023) weak-to-strong paper; OpenAI open-source code. Scaling Laws for Scalable Oversight (April 2025) provides quantitative framework to compare against.

# Task Domain Variation in Weak-to-Strong Generalization: Coding vs. Reasoning vs. Factual QA

**Problem:** The original weak-to-strong paper used a limited set of tasks. It is unknown whether the results generalize across fundamentally different task types.

**Direction:** Replicate the weak-to-strong setup on three different task types: factual QA, mathematical reasoning, and code generation. Compare the degree of generalization across domains using the same model pairs.

**Why it matters:** If weak-to-strong generalization is domain-dependent, safety guarantees from one domain cannot be transferred to others, which has major implications for deployment.

**Relevant context:** Burns et al. (2023); open problem of easy-to-hard generalization; OpenAI open-source weak-to-strong code.

# Varying Overseer Accuracy Rate: What is the Minimum Overseer Quality Needed for Useful Supervision?

**Problem:** There is no known threshold below which weak overseer accuracy makes supervision useless or counterproductive. Finding this threshold would define the minimum viable oversight bar.

**Direction:** Simulate overseers at various fixed accuracy levels (50%, 60%, 70%, 80%, 90%, 100%) by corrupting ground-truth labels. Train student models under each regime and plot downstream performance.

**Why it matters:** Understanding the minimum viable oversight accuracy is needed to determine whether current human oversight or weak model oversight meets the bar for safe training.

**Relevant context:** Open problem: systematic oversight errors; reward hacking of oversight signals.
